books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.text:
“...That all persons born in the United States and not subject to any foreign power, excluding Indians not taxed, are hereby declared to be citizens of the United States; and such citizens, of every race and color, without regard to any previous condition of slavery or involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall have the same right, in every State and Territory in the United States, to make and enforce contracts, to sue, be parties, and give evidence, to inherit, purchase, lease, sell, hold, and convey real and personal property, and to full and equal benefit of all laws and proceedings for the security of person and property, as is enjoyed by white citizens...”

—Civil Rights Act of 1866, Section 1, April 9, 1866
stimulus.source_note: Civil Rights Act of 1866, Section 1, April 9, 1866. Public domain. Wording verified against the Statutes at Large text (14 Stat. 27) as reproduced by the National Constitution Center. Leading and trailing ellipses mark omitted text.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: By declaring freedpeople citizens with the same rights as white citizens to make contracts and own property, the act most directly

rationales.A: Background: slavery had already ended everywhere with the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865.
rationales.B: Citizenship plus equal contract and property rights gave freedpeople a federal claim they could take to court. For the first time, Washington had a statute to use against Southern laws that singled out Black people.
rationales.C: Background: the act says nothing about voting; the vote came with the Fifteenth Amendment in 1870.
rationales.D: Background: military rule came a year later, with the Reconstruction Acts of 1867.
rationales.general:
1. The act does not just declare freedpeople free; it declares them citizens.
2. Citizenship carries a bundle of rights: contracts, property, courts, equal protection of the laws.
3. Background: before this act, a freedperson wronged in a Southern court had no federal law to appeal to.
4. Now Washington had a tool, and the courts had a standard.
Remember: a new right matters most when it comes with a way to enforce it.
